content: This period can range from a few minutes to as long as thirty years, as seen in cases of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. While the terms latent period and latency period are often used interchangeably with incubation period, a distinction is sometimes made. Specifically, the incubation period refers to the time between infection and the clinical onset of the disease, whereas the latent period refers to the time from infection to the point at which the individual becomes infectious to others. The relative length of these periods depends on the specific disease in question. In some cases, an individual may carry a disease-causing organism, such as Streptococcus bacteria in the throat, without displaying any symptoms. Whether or not the individual is capable of transmitting the disease to others during the incubation period depends on the nature of the disease. The length of incubation periods can vary significantly and is typically expressed as a range. When possible, it is ideal to report the mean incubation period along with the 10th and 90th percentiles, though such detailed data is not always available. In some instances, the mean incubation period must be inferred due to limited data. Additionally, for many diseases, the incubation period tends to be longer in adults compared to children or infants.
